slides.title: Dhunuchi naach: the dance of smoke and dhak
slides.sub: What it is, when to see it, how to stay safe

slides.title: What's in a dhunuchi
slides.body: A clay bowl on a short stem, filled with dried coconut husk that smoulders steadily and fed with dhuno, a resin traditionally from the sal tree, for thick, sweet white smoke. It grows out of the arati.

slides.title: No fixed steps
slides.body: Dancers sway, turn and raise the burner to the goddess, following the dhaki as the dhaki follows them. Skilled ones hold a dhunuchi in their teeth, or balance one on the head while dancing with two more.

slides.line: Follow the dhak: the rhythm quickens as the arati builds

slides.title: Saptami, Ashtami, Navami
slides.body: At the evening arati, whose time varies by puja and tithi. Navami night, the last before the goddess leaves, is the most intense. Ask the organisers, or arrive early in the evening and wait.

slides.title: Before you pick one up
items: Hold it by the stem, or with a folded cloth
Tuck in sari ends, dupattas and hair
Dance only where there is room
Keep water or sand nearby for embers
Watching? Stand back, keep children close

caption.en:
Dhunuchi naach at Durga Puja 2026 in Kolkata: what it is and where to see it 🥁

A clay burner of smouldering coconut husk and dhuno, raised to the goddess to the beat of the dhak. It belongs to the evening arati from Saptami to Navami, and peaks on Navami night.

There are no fixed steps. Dancers follow the dhaki and the dhaki follows them. The best hold one in their teeth.

The burner holds live embers, so tuck in sari ends and hair, hold it by the stem and dance only where there is room.

slides.title: Pujo with kids and elderly parents
slides.sub: Quieter hours, fewer pandals, a plan before you go

slides.title: Go when the city is quieter
slides.body: Dawn to about 9 am is the calmest, even at famous pandals, and cooler too. Late morning to afternoon is moderate but hotter. Skip about 6 pm to midnight, Saptami to Navami, at the big names.

slides.title: Pick easier pandals
slides.body: Big theme pandals are best early in the morning. Salt Lake's block pujas sit on wider roads. Your own para puja is often easiest of all: no travel, familiar faces and a place to sit.

slides.title: A lost-child plan
items: A card with your number in a secure pocket
A photo of each child that morning
Lost? Stop, stay put, go to a volunteer
A meeting point agreed at every pandal
Hold hands in queues and at gates

slides.title: A carrier beats a stroller
slides.body: Pandal entrances often have steps, narrow paths and dense queues, and some don't allow strollers inside. A carrier or sling is usually easier; a light folding stroller helps on wide roads.

slides.title: Plan the rests
slides.body: Plan stops at a café, a park or a quiet family-puja courtyard. A light folding stool helps while waiting, but not in queues. Some pujas have seating for older visitors, especially during aarti.

slides.title: Ask at the gate
slides.bn: আলাদা গেট আছে কি না জিজ্ঞেস করুন
slides.body: Some committees provide a separate entrance, ramp or priority line for elderly and disabled visitors, but not all. Ask volunteers on arrival and go at quiet hours. India's emergency number is 112.

caption.en:
Durga Puja in Kolkata with kids and elderly parents: the hours, the pandals and a lost-child plan 🪔

Go when the city's quieter. Dawn to about 9 am is the calmest time, even at famous pandals. We'd skip about 6 pm to midnight from Saptami to Navami with toddlers, wheelchairs or frail relatives.

Give every child a card with your phone number. Take a photo of them that morning, and agree a meeting point at each pandal. A carrier usually beats a stroller, and some committees run a separate entrance for elderly and disabled visitors, so ask a volunteer.

slides.title: Agomoni: the songs of Uma coming home
slides.sub: Why pujo feels like a homecoming

slides.title: Slayer in scripture, daughter in song
slides.body: In scripture Durga is the ten-armed slayer of Mahishasura. In song she is Uma, a young married woman coming home to her parents. Agomoni songs welcome her; Bijoya songs mourn her going.

slides.title: Once a year, three days
slides.body: Uma has married Shiva, who lives far away on Kailash. She may visit her mother Menaka and father Giriraj Himalaya only once a year, for the three days of the puja, bringing her children.

slides.title: Menaka waits
slides.body: Menaka dreams of Uma and wakes weeping. She frets over a son-in-law who smears himself with ash and owns nothing. Then word comes that Uma has arrived, and the songs burst into joy.

slides.title: Navami night, don't end
slides.body: The three days fly. Menaka pleads with the night of Navami not to end, because dawn brings Dashami, and Shiva will come to take Uma away.

slides.title: Ramprasad and Kamalakanta
slides.body: The songs belong to Bengal's Shakta padavali. Ramprasad Sen and Kamalakanta Bhattacharya are the poets most linked with them, though many songs have uncertain authorship: a shared inheritance.

slides.line: In the weeks before pujo, radio and TV run Agomoni programmes

slides.title: Does your family sing an Agomoni?

caption.en:
Agomoni songs: why Durga Puja feels like Uma coming home 🎶

In song, Durga is Uma, a married daughter who may visit her mother Menaka and father Giriraj once a year, for the three days of the puja. Agomoni songs welcome her home. Bijoya songs, around Navami night and Dashami, mourn her going.

They grew out of the Shakta padavali of the 18th and 19th centuries, linked most with Ramprasad Sen and Kamalakanta Bhattacharya. You don't need Bengali to feel them; the melodies carry it.
